title: Git Commands Cheat Sheet

introduction.heading: The Git Commands You'll Actually Use Every Day
introduction.description: Saving your work in Git is a two-step process - staging, then committing - and everything below builds around that. Use this as a quick reference for checking your setup, starting a project, saving snapshots of your work, reviewing history, and undoing mistakes.

prerequisites: Git installed locally (run git --version to confirm)
A terminal open in a project folder - either an existing repository or one you're about to create

steps.title: Check Your Setup
steps.description: Before you do anything else, confirm Git is installed and see what identity and configuration it's using. Settings can live at three levels - system (every user), global (you, on this machine), and local (just this one repository) - and local always wins over global, which wins over system.
steps.note: git config --list --global is the one you'll reach for most - it shows your name, email, and editor without any repo-specific noise mixed in.

steps.title: Start a Project
steps.description: Before Git can track anything, it needs to know which folder to watch. There are two ways to begin: create a brand-new, empty repository, or copy one that already exists.
steps.note: git init creates a hidden .git folder that stores all history. git clone copies that folder plus every commit from a remote - use it when a project already exists on GitHub.

steps.title: Check the Status
steps.description: This is the command you'll run constantly - it shows exactly where every file stands right now.
steps.note: Red = changed but not staged yet. Green = staged and ready to be committed.

steps.title: Stage Your Changes
steps.description: Staging is the "loading area" between your edits and a saved commit - it lets you choose exactly what goes into the next snapshot instead of committing everything blindly.
steps.note: Think of it like packing items into a box before taping it shut: git add puts something in the box, git commit tapes it and puts it on the shelf.

steps.title: Commit Your Changes
steps.description: A commit is a permanent, named snapshot of whatever is currently staged.
steps.note: Write messages that describe what changed and why ("Add login button"), not vague ones ("fix") - future you (and git log) will thank you.

steps.title: Push to a Remote
steps.description: Once you're happy with a commit, send it to a remote repository (like GitHub) so it's backed up and visible to others.
steps.note: <branch> is just a placeholder - swap it for whatever you're actually on, e.g. git push -u origin main. No remote yet? Check with git remote -v and add one with git remote add origin <url>. The -u flag is only needed the first time you push a branch - after that, plain git push remembers where to go.

steps.title: Inspect History
steps.description: Once you have a few commits, these commands let you see who changed what, when, and exactly which lines.
steps.note: git log and git diff open in a pager if the output is long - **press Q** to quit back to your terminal. git diff on its own compares your working files to the last commit; add a commit range (e.g. git diff HEAD~1) to compare two points further back in history.

steps.title: Undo & Discard Changes
steps.description: Everyone makes mistakes - these are the three most common ways to walk them back.
steps.note: git checkout <commit-id> puts you in a read-only "detached HEAD" state - fine for looking around, but create a branch first if you want to make changes there.

gettingStarted.heading: Quick Checklist
steps: git config --list --global - check your identity and config
git init or git clone <url> - start or copy a repository
git status - run this before and after every change
git add . - stage everything you've changed
git commit -m "comment" - save a snapshot with a message
git push - send your commits to the remote
git log --oneline / git diff - review history and exact changes
git restore <file> - discard a mistake before it's committed
